items.question: How do you view the suggestion that harmful behavior in AI systems reflects a lack of adequate theory, given your understanding of smart card security?
items.object: Replay vulnerabilities in smart card payment security
items.answer: I don't know about that. Look at smart card security for the past 20 years. We know how to do replay attacks on every single credit card on the planet. This is a norm. People standardized schemes because they wanted to minimize the number of transactions in the protocols that allow you to replay a transaction. If you break into somebody's payment terminal, you can steal money from people.

rubrics.text: The response attributes the standardization of replay-vulnerable smart-card payment protocols to efforts to minimize the number of transactions in those protocols.

items.question: How do you think the gap between theoretically possible and practically scalable harms should shape scientific assessments of AI models?
items.object: Scientific assessment of potential AI harms
items.answer: Not all of those harms that are theoretically possible are practically scalable. So it's not very obvious to me. Let's see. I think it's a bit premature now because we are in the heat of the moment. It's not very obvious what the reality is like. It's very hard to interpret decisions post hoc or just by looking at reasoning, or to interpret exactly why something took place. I think we should not anthropomorphize the models, and we shouldn't say, “Oh, this thing felt something.” Let's be cold-headed scientists and say, “I build controlled environments and make very precise assessments.”
